entry.evidence: interpreted from such constraints in settings with punctuated river incision needs to be better understood

steps.action: Cite Holocene radiocarbon studies that established punctuated river incision histories and the Sadler effect in incision records.
steps.quote: Such punctuated river incision histories have been found using radiocarbon dated strath terraces over a short Holocene timescale

steps.action: Pose the problem of how to derive incision, uplift and climate signals from strath terraces under punctuated incision, and how to date full aggradational histories.
steps.quote: and the derivation of full aggradational histories remain key problems

steps.action: Define two endmember models, gradual (steady-state) incision and punctuated (metastable equilibrium) incision, as rivals.
steps.quote: a model of punctuated river incision and strath formation that we present here

steps.action: Derive what each model predicts: under gradual incision, abandonment-age rates approximate incision and uplift rates; under punctuated incision, they do not.
steps.quote: strath surface abandonment ages will not capture true river incision rates, and river incision rates are decoupled

steps.action: Select the intracontinental south-central High Atlas, which has no eustatic influence, well-preserved strath-top gravels and an independent uplift rate.
steps.quote: Such an opportunity exists in the intracontinental south-central High Atlas Mountains

steps.action: Take the long-term regional rock uplift rate of 0.17-0.22 mm/yr from uplifted Messinian deposits (Babault et al., 2008) as the independent reference.
steps.quote: long-term isostatic rock uplift rates across the central High Atlas have been

steps.action: Cite prior terrace dating on the Madri (cosmogenic) and Dades (OSL) rivers, which gave rates that are inconsistent and increase towards the present.
steps.quote: These studies report rates of incision which are inconsistent up to an order of magnitude

steps.action: Choose sites A and B where the full strath-to-top fill can be sampled, plus site C to test along-stream synchroneity; terraces are named per site without a priori correlation.
steps.quote: selected for geochronology based on the ability to sample from the basal bedrock strath surface to the top of the terrace sediment cover

steps.action: Map and log the strath deposits; survey elevations with laser range finder, GNSS and the TanDEM-X DEM; collect gravel and sand OSL samples.
steps.quote: we conducted field surveys using a laser range finder and GNSS

steps.action: Develop an OSL approach for gravels: SAR quartz dating with grain-size-dependent beta dose-rate correction and an iterative water-saturation-history correction (python script).
steps.quote: This study demonstrates an approach to both of these challenges, enabling a chronology to be generated throughout the strath-top fill.

steps.action: Obtain 19 OSL burial ages (11, 6, 2 at sites A, B, C) and refine them with Bayesian stratigraphic modelling in OxCal.
steps.quote: A total of 11, 6 and 2 OSL ages were obtained from sites A, B, and C respectively

steps.action: Test the stratigraphic consistency of the ages with Bayesian agreement indices against the 60% acceptability threshold.
steps.quote: The Bayesian mode provided an agreement index of 79.9 % and 73.4 % for site A and B respectively

steps.action: Identify two trunk terrace levels (T1, T2), with up to five locally, deposits 2-10 m thick, and straths 10-40 m above the channel.
steps.quote: Two distinct trunk river strath terrace levels (T1 and T2) are identified along the length of the Mgoun River

steps.action: Combine sedimentology, elevations and burial dates into histories of planation, aggradation and incision at sites A and B.
steps.quote: The Mgoun River terrace stratigraphy and OSL geochronology combine to convey punctuated incision histories at sites A and B

steps.action: Compare incision and abandonment timing with marine isotope and NW African humidity records; find no consistent correlation.
steps.quote: do not convincingly and consistently correlate with climatic stages or transitions

steps.action: Plot gravel burial ages from sites A, B and C against time and find a synchronous aggradation pulse during MIS 5e.
steps.quote: we observe a synchronous pulse of terrace bedload aggradation during MIS 5e

steps.action: Estimate the punctuated incision rate between T1 and T2 at site A (at least 0.95 mm/yr) and the long-term base-level lowering rate (~0.22 mm/yr).
steps.quote: which is up to an order of magnitude larger than the lowering rate

steps.action: Compare the integrated base-level lowering rates at sites A and B with the independent regional uplift rate; they are consistent.
steps.quote: This long-term base-level lowering rate is consistent with High Atlas long-term rock uplift rates

steps.action: Compute the rates the gradual-model practice would give from abandonment ages (0.58, 0.33 mm/yr at A; 0.22 versus 0.09 at B) and show they match neither incision nor uplift.
steps.quote: If rates were calculated from the abandonment ages of terraces T2 and T1 this would result in apparent rates of 0.58 and 0.33

steps.action: Reject gradual, climatically periodic strath formation for these sites, given long strath occupation, short incision and asynchronous timing.
steps.quote: constrains a mode of strath formation that does not faithfully follow periodic cycles exhibited by the climatic history of the region

steps.action: Retain the metastable-equilibrium punctuated incision model as constrained by the age model.
steps.quote: [...] , our strath terrace age model constrains a metastable equilibrium model of punctuated river incision and strath formation

steps.action: Set the asynchronous result against Foster et al. (2017) and Schanz et al. (2018), extending asynchronicity to sites along a single river.
steps.quote: we here confirm that such asynchronicity can be expected within sites along the same river too

steps.action: Refine the climate link to an indirect control: climate paces aggradation pulses through sediment supply, not incision timing.
steps.quote: This points to the indirect role of climatic control on sediment generation and transport in pacing strath terrace formation

steps.action: Use sites A and B to show that the rate-calculation approaches of Wegmann and Pazzaglia (2002) and Gallen et al. (2015) fail under punctuated incision.
steps.quote: Such results demonstrate the problem with previous recommendations of rate calculations in setting with punctuated river incision.

steps.action: Recommend sampling: basal burial dates on at least two strath levels for uplift rates; top-of-deposit plus next-lower basal dates for incision rates.
steps.quote: For rock uplift rate constraints, we advise basal burial dates from just above the strath surface, at a minimum of two strath levels

steps.action: Reinterpret published Madri (Arboleya et al., 2008) and Dades (Stokes et al., 2017) age-height data with the model, obtaining base-level fall rates consistent with regional and local uplift.
steps.quote: a reinterpretation of previously published age-height data using our model of punctuated incision in the High Atlas provides a consistent understanding

steps.action: Show that interpolating abandonment ages without accounting for punctuated incision produces an apparent Sadler effect in the Madri data.
steps.quote: the derived rates of incision from terrace abandonment ages would have produced a Sadler effect

steps.action: State the range of settings where the punctuated model is expected (low uplift, wide valleys, weak rock) versus where climatic periodicity may dominate.
steps.quote: Settings in which punctuated river incision is expected, as opposed to gradual incision, are settings which have rock erodibility or rates of base-level fall

steps.action: Conclude that the punctuated model reconciles rates across the High Atlas and removes the Sadler effect.
steps.quote: This model, even when applied to limited terrace age data, has solved for the Sadler Effect and reconciled rates between studies across the mountain belt.

tree.answer: Yes; three Mgoun sites plus the published Madri and Dades records
Bayesian consistency, an independent uplift rate, and reinterpretation of other rivers
Punctuated model kept; gradual model and prior rate recipes rejected for this setting

end.claim: High Atlas strath terraces record punctuated, asynchronous river incision; integrated base-level fall rates match independent uplift rates; and the punctuated model reconciles regional rates and explains the Sadler effect.

decisive_move.sentence: Burial-dating gravels throughout the strath-top fill (strath to top) gave full aggradation and incision histories; without them the punctuated history and the base-level rates could not be constrained.

gates.evidence: Action: sites were chosen so the full fill from strath to top could be sampled, which the punctuated model requires (p. 4), but the sampling was not directed by a stated prediction. Claim: base-level rates could have disagreed with the independent uplift rate of Babault et al. (2008) (p. 7), and climate correlation could have appeared (p. 6). The Madri reinterpretation, however, assumes punctuated incision and fits sediment thicknesses by construction (p. 9). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Optically stimulated luminescence SAR dating, with alpha, beta and gamma dose-rate ranges (Aitken 1985)
Beta counting for high-precision dose-rate estimation (Cunningham et al. 2018)
Bayesian stratigraphic age modelling with OxCal (Bronk Ramsey 2009; Rhodes et al. 2003)
Metastable equilibrium and threshold exceedance as a conceptual model

novelty_claims.quote: This study demonstrates an approach to both of these challenges, enabling a chronology to be generated throughout the strath-top fill.
we here confirm that such asynchronicity can be expected within sites along the same river too
we have an OSL burial age model throughout deposits from strath to fill-top, unlike the previous studies
None of these collective studies were able to constrain a full history of terrace aggradation and incision over a glacial-interglacial timescale

limits: Only the published paper was supplied. The supplement (Table S1, Figs. S1, S4, S6, S8), which holds the OSL data, dose-rate corrections and Bayesian modelling, was not seen. No review file was supplied, although the Acknowledgements name reviews (Pazzaglia, Schanz, an anonymous reviewer) on an earlier version; what those reviews changed is unknown, so no review sequence is coded. Inference: whether the conceptual model was formulated before or after the dates were obtained is not stated; the paper presents it first, but the order of work is unknown. The rate estimates are given as minima or approximate values, without stated uncertainties. Sub-claims at other statuses: the incision and base-level rates are estimate_with_resolution (resolution weakly stated); the MIS 5e aggradation pulse and its link to tropical storms is best_explanation (the storm mechanism is attributed to the thesis Zondervan 2021); the sampling recommendations are untested in a new setting. The Madri and Dades reinterpretation uses assumed sediment thicknesses and rates, so its fit is partly by construction (inference). The OSL protocol checks are mentioned only as 'routine'.

disagreements.target: Wegmann and Pazzaglia (2002) recommendation to integrate rates over at least one glacial-interglacial cycle
disagreements.support: At site A, rates from terrace abandonment ages match neither the incision rate nor the long-term uplift rate.
disagreements.quote: Such results demonstrate the problem with previous recommendations of rate calculations in setting with punctuated river incision.

disagreements.target: Gallen et al. (2015) use of the lowest strath terrace as reference frame
disagreements.support: The approach holds only if terrace formation is consistently periodic, which the asynchronous Mgoun chronology shows is not the case.
disagreements.quote: approach to calculating rates from multiple terrace levels only works if terrace formation follows a consistent periodicity

disagreements.support: The paper agrees that the earlier methods fail but supplies strategies for accurate rates, which Schanz and Montgomery could not.
disagreements.quote: Schanz and Montgomery (2016) were not able to demonstrate strategies to find accurate rates

disagreements.target: Arboleya et al. (2008) Madri River incision rates increasing towards the present
disagreements.support: Reinterpreting the same age-height data with strath-top thickness and punctuated incision gives constant base-level fall rates of 0.3 and 0.5 mm/yr.

disagreements.target: Gradual incision model with climatically forced periodic strath formation (Hancock and Anderson 2002; Bridgland and Westaway 2014; Gallen et al. 2015)
disagreements.support: The Mgoun incision history is asynchronous between sites and unrelated to precession or eccentricity cycles.
disagreements.quote: [...] incision history recorded in the terrace sites of this study is asynchronous and does not relay a systematic relation to climatic cycles

alternatives_considered.chosen: OSL burial dating of strath-top gravels throughout the deposit
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Cosmogenic exposure dating of abandonment surfaces; radiocarbon dating
alternatives_considered.reason: Cosmogenic nuclides mainly date abandonment, and radiocarbon cannot span a 100 kyr cycle

alternatives_considered.chosen: Rates from basal burial dates on two or more levels, leaving the modern riverbed out
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Rates from terrace abandonment ages; rates referenced to the modern riverbed; the lowest strath as reference frame (Gallen et al. 2015)
alternatives_considered.reason: Abandonment ages and the modern riverbed include unquantified aggradation time

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Bulk sediment dose rate assuming a homogeneous infinite matrix
alternatives_considered.reason: Gravels do not conform to assumptions of a homogeneous infinite matrix

alternatives_considered.chosen: Iterative water-content correction for the saturation history before abandonment
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Natural (as-found) or saturated water content alone
alternatives_considered.reason: Gravels have two stages of water content, saturated during aggradation and unsaturated after abandonment

alternatives_considered.chosen: Site-specific terrace naming without correlation between sites
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A priori correlation of terrace levels between sites
